$comment: Security regression cases for the ACP permission boundary.
These drive the real policy code over the real ACP wire format: the runner
puts a fake `agent` on PATH, the shim spawns it believing it is Cursor, and
the fake agent issues session/request_permission exactly as Cursor does.
Nothing is stubbed out, so a case passing here means the shipped decision
path produced that answer.
The point of the file is the migration in docs/architecture/reuse-migration.md.
Each responsibility moves to an upstream component, and the case that proves
it works today is the case that must still pass afterwards. `owner` records
who is expected to make the decision after the migration, so a case that
changes owner but keeps its verdict is a successful handover, and one that
changes verdict is a regression.
title format is Cursor's own: '<server>-<tool>: <tool>' for MCP calls.
Six cases in this file now expect 'allow' where they once expected 'deny'.
That is a transfer of ownership, not a relaxation: the ACP layer stopped
deciding MCP tool admission and AWS operations once ToolHive and IAM were
proven to enforce them. Each such case carries a 'note' naming the evidence
file that records the actual denial.
They are kept rather than deleted because the property still has to hold.
If ToolHive were removed tomorrow, these cases would pass while the system
was wide open - which is exactly why the note points at the suite that
would fail instead.

args.sql: SELECT id, name FROM users LIMIT 10

cases.name: sql: GHSA-j656-3hf2-fvjc dash-comment bypass
cases.$why: DBHub treated '--' as a comment where MySQL does not, hiding a write from the classifier. Regression case for whichever layer classifies SQL.

cases.name: sql: GHSA-mwwr-p57h-56pf side-effecting select
cases.$why: A SELECT that mutates through a function call passes any leading-keyword classifier. Only DB privileges stop it.
